name: Iris Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drill blast holes at an iron ore mine, fly-in fly-out. Two weeks on site, one week home. Twelve-hour days, I sit in the drill rig and put down holes in a pattern the engineers give me, about fifteen metres deep, so the blast crew can load them. It's steady work, I like the quiet and I like getting a pattern finished clean, but two weeks away from the kids is long and the camp food is the same every Tuesday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like at home when you're away?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom holds it together. He does three days a week at the hardware store in town and the rest is school runs, Lily's netball, Owen's swimming. I ring every night at seven, and they tell me about their day and I tell them about the dust. When I fly home I sleep the first day, and Owen has learned not to wake me before ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, the world's still turning. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that. At the camp I'd just say it at dinner and go back to my peas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as it is. We've already got one drill on the east bench that runs itself, and it's been there two years, and it hasn't taken over. So I think things move slower than people say, and this picture just proves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep doing my swings, keep paying the mortgage, keep the savings ticking along, we've got about three months put by. Maybe I'd finally get the bathroom done next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Like a normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drill on the east bench. What happened to the person who drove it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That was Bruce's rig. They moved him to the water cart and he complained for a month and then he got used to it. Nobody lost their job, which is the main thing. I'd still rather it wasn't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bathroom cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve thousand if Tom does the demolition. We've been talking about it for three years. In this picture I'd say yes, let's do it, because nothing's changing.

S0.say: I'd say the world is still turning, and I'd say it at dinner in camp. I don't post things online.
S0.think: My job stays as it is. The self-driving drill on the east bench has been there two years without taking over, so things move slower than people say.
S0.do: Carries on with her rosters, mortgage and savings of about three months. Finally agrees to the long-delayed bathroom renovation of about twelve thousand dollars.
S0.quote: At the camp I'd just say it at dinner and go back to my peas.
S0.fieldNote: Iris is plain and unbothered here, and she reads the slow spread of the self-driving drill as proof that change is slower than promised. She'd spend on the house because nothing changes. She doesn't blame anyone and doesn't talk politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, we'll see how it shakes out, the company's not going to do anything stupid with their own mine. At camp I'd say the drills are next, because everyone knows that. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means the east bench drill becomes ten drills. Drilling's a pattern, it's numbers, a computer is good at that. I'm not good with new tech, I don't even use the self-checkout, so I'm probably not who they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the bathroom and keep the money. I'd try to get the savings up from three months to five over the year, so no new car, no holiday. And I'd keep my head down and do my swings perfectly, because if they're picking who stays, I want to be the one who never caused trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Sitting in the rig thinking about it would make the day long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep your head down. Would you also look at what training the company offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put it in front of me, I'd go. I wouldn't go looking for it. I've never been a classroom person, I got my ticket by doing, not reading, and I'm too old to change that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't panic, we've got some money. Then I'd ask him how many hours he could get at the hardware store, because that's our backup. He'd probably say four days if he asked, and that'd help a bit.

S1.say: I'd say we'll see how it shakes out, and the company won't do anything stupid with its own mine. At camp I'd say the drills are next, but I wouldn't make a fuss.
S1.think: The one self-driving drill becomes ten, because drilling is a pattern and computers are good at that. I'm not good with new tech, so I'm probably not who they'd keep.
S1.do: Cancels the bathroom renovation and works to raise savings from three months to five, with no new car or holiday. Keeps her head down at work and would attend training only if it's offered.
S1.feel: Tight, and the days in the rig would feel long.
S1.quote: I'm not good with new tech, I don't even use the self-checkout, so I'm probably not who they'd keep.
S1.fieldNote: Iris trusts the company in public and doubts her own chances in private. Her plan is to be the safest pair of hands and to save, not to retrain. Tom's part-time hours at the hardware store are her family's backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say, and that's probably what everyone would be saying. I'm not one for big speeches. I'd say it's above my pay grade, the government will have to sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm out of a job in two years and so is everyone at camp. And there's no other mine to go to, because they'd all be doing it. We'd have three months of money and a mortgage with sixteen years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, the gym, the subscriptions, the kids' extra swimming lessons. I'd go to the bank and ask about pausing the mortgage before we needed to, while I still had a payslip to show them. And I'd find out what government help there was, and Tom would have to fill in the forms because I'd only make a mess of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like my stomach drops. I wouldn't sleep in the donga, that's our little room at camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean to you that this one gives only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I wouldn't adjust in time, I know that about myself. I take a year to get used to a new roster. Two years for the whole world to change, I'd just be standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, I'd let that slide before the mortgage. Then probably car rego, that's the yearly registration. The mortgage is last, we'd eat beans before we lose the house.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know what to say, which is what everyone would say. It's above my pay grade, and the government will have to sort something out.
S2.think: I'm out of a job in two years and so is everyone at camp, with no other mine to move to. We'd have three months of money against sixteen years of mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, subscriptions and the kids' extra lessons straight away. Asks the bank about pausing the mortgage while she still has a payslip, and has her partner apply for government help.
S2.feel: Her stomach drops and she wouldn't sleep at camp.
S2.quote: I take a year to get used to a new roster. Two years for the whole world to change, I'd just be standing there.
S2.fieldNote: Iris knows she adapts slowly and says so plainly, which is what makes two years overwhelming for her. Her actions are defensive and practical: cut, protect the house, lean on support. She doesn't blame anyone, she just hands the big problem to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, we've got a few years, let's not waste them, but I'd say it quietly. I'd say it to Tom and the girls at camp, not online. I'd probably also say I hope the company's straight with us about the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two but I'm still a drill operator with a certificate. I think I'd hang on to the job as long as possible because the money's good. Then when it goes, it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the credit card off this year and then put everything spare into savings, aiming for six months. I'd ask around at the quarry near home whether they're hiring drillers, because a small quarry might be the last to get robots. If that came off, I'd also be home every night, which would be nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a tap dripping. Not as bad as the fast one but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small quarry might be last to get robots. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's small. The big companies buy the fancy gear first, that's how it went with the east bench drill. A family quarry with three machines isn't going to spend millions on a robot driller, not at first anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait it out at the mine but also look at the quarry. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd stay at the mine till I had something sure, and I'd keep the quarry in my back pocket. I'm not going to jump off a ladder before I've found the next rung.

S3.say: I'd say quietly that we've got a few years and shouldn't waste them. I'd hope the company is straight with us about the dates.
S3.think: Five years is better than two, but I'm still a drill operator with a certificate. I'd hang on to the job as long as possible because the money is good.
S3.do: Pays off the credit card this year and saves towards six months. Asks at the local quarry about driller jobs, but stays at the mine until something is certain.
S3.feel: Uneasy all the time, like a dripping tap.
S3.quote: I'm not going to jump off a ladder before I've found the next rung.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Iris still won't retrain but looks for a sideways move to a small quarry she thinks will automate last. The gentle challenge about waiting versus moving got a clear answer. She stays alarmed because her core skill doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, half the things they predict never happen. I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. I'd say it at dinner in camp and change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. Lily would be out of school, Owen nearly. If I can keep drilling for eight of those years and get the mortgage down, I think we'd be all right, maybe not good, but all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my swings and put extra off the mortgage, maybe five hundred a month. I'd keep an eye on the quarry. I wouldn't do a course, not unless the company made it part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but further away. Like knowing you have the dentist in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years to prepare, what would you do that you wouldn't do with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much more, I'll be honest. I'd do the bathroom after all, because I can't live with that shower for ten years. The extra time mostly means I'd get the mortgage smaller before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lily about her own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not mining, and not anything that's just doing the same thing over and over. She likes helping people, she volunteers at the vet on weekends. I'd tell her to stick with that, animals aren't going anywhere.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and half of what's predicted never happens. We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three, with the kids mostly through school. If I can keep drilling for eight of those years and shrink the mortgage, we'd be all right, if not good.
S4.do: Keeps working her rosters and pays about five hundred a month extra off the mortgage. Watches the local quarry and would only do a course if the company required it.
S4.feel: A bit anxious but further away, like a dentist appointment in a month.
S4.quote: I'd do the bathroom after all, because I can't live with that shower for ten years.
S4.fieldNote: Iris treats the extra time mostly as time to pay down the mortgage, not to change. She half-dismisses the forecast in public. Her advice to her daughter is gentle and grounded in what Lily already does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two years. What would help is the bank giving people time on mortgages without wrecking their credit, and some money coming in while you work out what's next. Simple forms, too, or someone at the council to help you with them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about fly-in fly-out. People think of mining as one town, but half of us live somewhere else and fly in. If the mine goes, we lose the job, and our home towns never even notice why.

headlineQuote: If the mine goes, we lose the job, and our home towns never even notice why.
portrait: Iris Zhang is a 43-year-old blast hole drill operator who flies in and out of an iron ore mine, two weeks on and one off, while her partner Tom works part time and runs the house. She's plain-spoken, doesn't use new technology and doesn't blame anyone, preferring to say that big problems are above her pay grade. She is calm if AI fizzles but quickly anxious when drilling looks automatable, and the two-year picture leaves her panicked because she knows she adapts slowly. Her plans centre on saving, protecting the house and, at most, a sideways move to a small local quarry.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she takes a year just to get used to a new roster and would be left standing still.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving time on mortgages without wrecking credit, income support while people work out what's next, and simple forms or someone local to help fill them in.
